pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 1: Components of Computers and Computer Systems

In your final JHS year you will look at where computing is heading: quantum and perceptual computing, wearable and paper-like displays, and storage that lives in the cloud or even in light. You will also personalise Windows and manage device drivers like an IT technician.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.1.1.1** Identify parts of a computer and technology tools.
- **B9.1.1.2** Demonstrate the use of the desktop.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.1.1.1.1** Discuss the trends in the next generation of computers.
- **B9.1.1.1.2** Examine the concept of perceptual computing.
- **B9.1.1.1.3** Discuss the uses of output devices such as wearable displays, e-paper, e-books and Kindle.
- **B9.1.1.1.4** Describe storage systems: network and cloud storage, smart cards, holographic storage, storage for large computer systems (home and media servers).
- **B9.1.1.2.1** Explore personalisation of the computer.
- **B9.1.1.2.2** Identify and use file management techniques (drivers and hardware).

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 1.1 Trends in the Next Generation of Computers
- 1.2 Perceptual Computing
- 1.3 Wearable Displays, E-Paper, E-Books and Kindle
- 1.4 Network, Cloud, Smart Card, Holographic and Large-System Storage
- 1.5 Personalising the Computer
- 1.6 Device Drivers and Plug-and-Play

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC7.3, CC7.5), Digital Literacy (DL5.1, DL5.3).

lessons.title: Trends in the Next Generation of Computers

pages.title: Trends in the Next Generation of Computers
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify features expected in the next generation of computers;
- describe Google’s Sycamore quantum computer and compare its processing power with supercomputers.
## Features expected in the next generation of computers
| **Trend** | **What to expect** |
|---|---|
| AI everywhere | Computers with built-in AI chips (NPUs, neural processing units) that run assistants, translation and image tools on the device; “AI PCs” are already sold |
| Quantum computing | Quantum processors working alongside classical supercomputers for chemistry, medicine, logistics and cryptography |
| Natural interaction (perceptual computing) | Control by voice, gesture, eye movement and facial expression, not only keyboard and mouse |
| Wearable and invisible computing | Smart glasses, watches, rings and clothing; computing built into homes, cars and cities (Internet of Things) |
| Cloud and edge computing | Most storage and heavy processing in data centres; quick local processing at the “edge” (e.g. in cars) |
| Smaller, faster, greener chips | Transistors only a few nanometres wide; 3D chip stacking; more energy-efficient designs |
| New materials and ideas | Optical (light-based) and neuromorphic (brain-like) chips; DNA and holographic storage in research |
| Stronger security and privacy | Biometrics, passwordless sign-in (passkeys) and post-quantum encryption |

pages.title: Sycamore compared with supercomputers
pages.body:
## Sycamore compared with supercomputers
A **supercomputer** is an extremely fast classical computer made of thousands of connected processors (CPUs and GPUs). Its speed is measured in **FLOPS** (floating-point operations per second): 1 petaflop = 10¹⁵ FLOPS; 1 exaflop = 10¹⁸ FLOPS. A **quantum computer** such as Sycamore uses qubits and is designed for a different kind of problem.
| **Machine** | **Type and processor** | **Size / power** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google Sycamore (2019) | Superconducting **quantum** processor | 54 qubits (53 used) | Did a random-sampling task in ~200 s that Google estimated would take Summit ~10,000 years |
| IBM Summit (fastest 2018–2020) | Classical: IBM POWER9 CPUs + NVIDIA V100 GPUs | ≈ 2.4 million cores; 148.6 petaflops | The supercomputer Google compared Sycamore with |
| El Capitan (USA) | Classical: AMD EPYC CPUs + AMD Instinct MI300A accelerators | ≈ 11.3 million cores; 1.809 exaflops | World No. 1 from November 2024 to June 2026 |
| LineShine (China) | Classical: CPU-only design with Chinese LingKun processors | ≈ 13.8 million cores; 2.198 exaflops | World No. 1 on the June 2026 TOP500 list |
| Google Willow (2024) | Superconducting **quantum** processor | 105 qubits | A benchmark in under 5 minutes estimated at 10²⁵ years on a classical supercomputer |

pages.title: Sycamore compared with supercomputers (continued)
pages.body: > 💡 **Think About It Is A Quantum Computer “Faster” Than A Supercomputer?** Only for **certain special problems**. Supercomputers can run any program: weather forecasts, engineering simulations, AI training. Quantum computers today are small, error-prone and must be kept colder than outer space. Their huge advantage appears only on tasks suited to quantum effects. Experts expect quantum and classical computers to work **together**. Check top500.org for the latest supercomputer rankings, which are updated every June and November.

pages.title: Perceptual Computing
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain perceptual computing;
- discuss its features and examples.
**Perceptual computing** means computers that can **perceive** (sense and understand) people and their surroundings the way humans do: by seeing, hearing and recognising touch and movement. Users interact naturally, using voice, gestures, facial expressions and eye movement. The term was popularised by **Intel** around 2013 with its 3D depth cameras (later called **Intel RealSense**).
| **Feature** | **Example** |
|---|---|
| Speech recognition and voice control | Voice assistants (Siri, Google Assistant, Alexa, Copilot); voice typing |
| Facial recognition | **Windows Hello** and **Face ID** sign-in; photo tagging |
| Gesture recognition | Waving to control a game (Microsoft Kinect), hand tracking in VR headsets, air gestures on some phones |
| Eye tracking | Controlling a computer with your eyes (Windows Eye Control, VR headsets); helps people with disabilities |
| Emotion and expression detection | Software that estimates if a driver is drowsy |
| 3D depth sensing | Depth cameras that measure distance for robots, AR and secure face unlock |
| Context awareness | A phone that silences itself when face-down or adjusts brightness to the room |

pages.title: Perceptual Computing (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity**
In groups, list every way you can control a smartphone without touching the screen (voice, face unlock, gestures, etc.). Present how each one is an example of perceptual computing, and give your views on the privacy issues raised by cameras and microphones that are always “listening”.

lessons.title: Wearable Displays, E-Paper, E-Books and Kindle

pages.title: Wearable Displays, E-Paper, E-Books and Kindle
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe wearable displays, e-paper and e-books;
- discuss their uses.
## Wearable displays
A **wearable display** is a screen worn on the body. **Smart glasses** and **head-mounted displays** show information in front of the eyes; **smartwatches** and fitness bands show information on the wrist.
| **Device** | **Description and uses** |
|---|---|
| Google Glass | Smart glasses with a tiny display above the right eye, a camera, voice control and Internet connection (launched 2013). Used by doctors, factory workers and technicians to see instructions hands-free. Google stopped selling the Enterprise Edition in 2023. |
| Newer smart glasses | Glasses with cameras, speakers and AI assistants (e.g. Ray-Ban Meta); some add small displays |
| Mixed-reality headsets | Apple Vision Pro, Meta Quest, Microsoft HoloLens: full displays for VR/AR/MR |
| Smartwatches and fitness bands | Time, messages, heart rate, steps, sleep, GPS, payments |
## E-paper (electronic paper)
[[fig:c9-f02|Figure 1: How e-paper displays text]]
**E-paper** is a display technology that looks like ink on paper. The best-known type, **E Ink**, uses millions of tiny **microcapsules** containing charged black and white particles. An electric field moves the particles to the top to form text and images. E-paper reflects light rather than glowing, so it is easy to read in sunlight, causes less eye strain, and uses power **only when the page changes**, so a battery can last for weeks.

pages.title: Wearable Displays, E-Paper, E-Books and Kindle (continued)
pages.body:
- **Uses:** e-readers, electronic shelf labels in supermarkets, bus and train timetables, some phones and watches, smart badges.
- **Limitations:** slow refresh (not good for video); most are black and white (colour versions exist but are paler).
## E-books and the Kindle
An **e-book** is an electronic version of a book that can be read on a screen or a dedicated handheld reading device (an **e-reader**). Formats include EPUB, PDF and Amazon’s Kindle formats. The **Amazon Kindle**, first released in the United States in **November 2007**, is a family of e-readers that use E Ink displays. The original Kindle could download e-books wirelessly through Amazon’s **Whispernet** service, which used Sprint’s EVDO mobile network.
| **Advantages of e-books** | **Disadvantages** |
|---|---|
| Thousands of books in one light device | Need a device and charging |
| Adjustable text size and built-in dictionary | Some books are not available or are expensive |
| Instant download; search inside the book | Licences may limit sharing and lending |
| Saves paper and storage space | Screen reading can be tiring on non-E Ink devices |
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection** Free e-books and readers’ apps (such as the **African Storybook** project and digital libraries) give Ghanaian learners access to stories in English and local languages on low-cost phones.

pages.title: Network, Cloud, Smart Card, Holographic and Large-System Storage
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe network and cloud storage, smart cards, holographic storage and large-system storage;
- explore cloud storage services;
- discuss the pros and cons of cloud storage.
## Network storage
**Network storage** keeps files on a storage device connected to a network so that many users and devices can share them. A **NAS (Network Attached Storage)** is a box with one or more hard disks that plugs into the router. Large organisations use a **SAN (Storage Area Network)**, a dedicated high-speed network of storage devices.
[[fig:c9-f03|Figure 2: A NAS or home media server shared over a LAN]]
## Storage systems for large computer systems: home servers and media servers
- A **home server** stores the family’s documents and photo backups and shares them on the home network.
- A **media server** stores films, music and photos and streams them to smart TVs, phones and computers (e.g. with Plex or Jellyfin software).
- **RAID** (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines several disks so that data survives if one disk fails, or so that the disks work faster.
- Banks, universities and companies use racks of servers, tape libraries and SANs in **data centres**.
## Cloud storage
**Cloud storage** means saving data on remote servers owned by a provider, accessed through the Internet from any device.

pages.title: Network, Cloud, Smart Card, Holographic and Large-System Storage (continued)
pages.body:
[[fig:c9-f04|Figure 3: Cloud storage and synchronisation]]
| **Service** | **Free storage (2026)** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|
| Google Drive | 15 GB (shared with Gmail and Google Photos) | Google Docs, Sheets, Slides; real-time collaboration |
| Microsoft OneDrive | 5 GB | Built into Windows and Microsoft 365 |
| Apple iCloud | 5 GB | iPhone, iPad, Mac backups |
| Dropbox | 2 GB | File sharing and sync |
Free storage amounts change from time to time; check each provider’s website.
| **Pros of cloud storage** | **Cons of cloud storage** |
|---|---|
| Access files from anywhere, on any device | Needs Internet access; data costs |
| Automatic backup: files survive if your phone is lost | Privacy concerns: data held by another company, possibly abroad |
| Easy sharing and collaboration | Risk of account hacking (use strong passwords and 2FA) |
| Pay only for the space you need; no hardware to buy | Subscription costs for large storage |
| Version history to restore older copies | Service outages or provider closure |
## Smart cards
A **smart card** is a plastic card with a built-in **microprocessor chip** (and memory) that can store data securely and carry out processing, such as checking a PIN or encrypting a transaction. **Contact** smart cards are inserted into a reader; **contactless** ones communicate by radio (NFC) when tapped.
- Bank debit and credit cards (EMV chip and contactless).
- SIM cards in phones.
- National ID cards: the **Ghana Card** issued by the National Identification Authority contains a chip.
- Staff access cards, transport cards and health insurance cards.

pages.title: Holographic storage
pages.body:
## Holographic storage
**Holographic storage** is a computer storage technology that uses beams of **laser light** to store data in **three dimensions** inside a crystal or special polymer, instead of only on a surface. Because data is recorded throughout the volume of the material, and whole pages of data can be read in one flash, it could store enormous amounts very quickly and last for decades. It is still mainly **experimental** (research by Microsoft and universities), but it shows the future direction of archival storage.
> 🧪 **Activity — Explore cloud storage**
1. Sign in to Google Drive or OneDrive with a school account.
2. Create a folder B9_Computing, upload a document, and open it on a phone.
3. Share the file with a classmate with **Viewer** access and another with **Editor** access. Compare what each can do.
4. Discuss in groups whether your school should store learners’ records in the cloud, considering pros and cons.

pages.title: Personalising the Computer
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.2.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- change desktop icons;
- change mouse pointers;
- personalise the background, colours and themes.
**Personalisation** means changing the appearance and behaviour of the computer to suit the user. In Windows 11 most options are in **Settings › Personalisation** (right-click the desktop › **Personalise**).
> 🪜 **Step by step — Changing desktop icons**
1. Open **Settings › Personalisation › Themes**.
2. Under **Related settings**, click **Desktop icon settings**.
3. Tick the icons to show on the desktop (Computer, User’s Files, Network, Recycle Bin, Control Panel).
4. Select an icon, click **Change Icon…**, choose a new picture and click **OK** then **Apply**.
5. To change a shortcut’s icon: right-click the shortcut › **Properties › Shortcut › Change Icon**. To change icon size, right-click the desktop › **View › Large/Medium/Small icons**.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Changing mouse pointers**
1. **Quick way:** **Settings › Accessibility › Mouse pointer and touch**: choose a pointer style (white, black, inverted, custom colour) and drag the **Size** slider.
2. **Pointer schemes:** **Settings › Bluetooth & devices › Mouse › Additional mouse settings** opens Mouse Properties.
3. Click the **Pointers** tab, choose a **Scheme** (e.g. Windows Black (large)) or select one pointer and click **Browse** to replace it.
4. On the **Pointer Options** tab, set pointer speed and turn on **Display pointer trails** if you wish. Click **Apply**, then **OK**.

pages.title: Personalising the Computer (continued)
pages.body:
| **Other personalisation options** | **Where** |
|---|---|
| Desktop background (picture, solid colour, slideshow) | Personalisation › Background |
| Accent colour, light/dark mode | Personalisation › Colours |
| Themes (background + colours + sounds + pointer) | Personalisation › Themes |
| Lock screen picture | Personalisation › Lock screen |
| Start menu layout and taskbar alignment | Personalisation › Start / Taskbar |
> 🛡️ **Safety first** On shared school computers, change settings only when your teacher allows it, and return them to normal afterwards.

pages.title: Device Drivers and Plug-and-Play
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.2.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify and explore device drivers;
- explain plug-and-play;
- install, update and delete drivers.
A **device driver** is a small program that allows the operating system to communicate with a specific hardware device. The OS sends general commands (e.g. “print this page”); the driver translates them into the exact instructions that particular device understands. Without the correct driver, a device may not work or may work poorly.
[[fig:c9-f05|Figure 4: A driver sits between the operating system and the hardware]]
| **Driver type** | **Controls** |
|---|---|
| Sound (audio) driver | Speakers, headphones, microphone (e.g. Realtek High Definition Audio) |
| Video graphics (display) driver | Graphics card and monitor: resolution, colours, 3D performance (Intel, AMD, NVIDIA) |
| Network driver | Wi-Fi and Ethernet adapters |
| Printer and scanner drivers | Printing and scanning features |
| Chipset, USB, Bluetooth, touchpad drivers | Motherboard and other devices |
## Plug-and-play
**Plug-and-play (PnP)** means that when you connect a device (e.g. a USB flash drive, mouse, printer or webcam), the operating system **automatically detects** it, finds and installs a suitable driver, and makes it ready to use, without the user having to configure anything manually. Windows has many drivers built in and downloads others through **Windows Update**.

pages.title: Device Drivers and Plug-and-Play (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Managing drivers with Device Manager**
1. Right-click **Start** › **Device Manager** (or run devmgmt.msc).
2. Expand a category such as **Sound, video and game controllers** or **Display adapters**. A **yellow warning triangle** means the device has a driver problem.
3. **Update:** right-click the device › **Update driver › Search automatically for drivers**. Also check **Settings › Windows Update › Advanced options › Optional updates › Driver updates**.
4. **Install** from the manufacturer: download the driver from the official website of the device or computer maker and run the installer; or choose **Update driver › Browse my computer for drivers**.
5. **Roll back** a bad update: right-click › **Properties › Driver › Roll Back Driver**.
6. **Delete (uninstall):** right-click › **Uninstall device**, tick **Attempt to remove the driver for this device** if offered, then restart. Windows may reinstall a basic driver automatically.
> 🛡️ **Safety first** Only download drivers from the **official manufacturer** or **Windows Update**. “Driver updater” programs from unknown websites often contain adware or malware. Ask your teacher before changing drivers on school computers.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. State **five** features expected in the next generation of computers.
2. Compare Google’s Sycamore with a classical supercomputer in terms of processor type and the problems each can solve.
3. Explain perceptual computing with **three** examples.
4. Describe how e-paper works and give **two** advantages.
5. State **three** pros and **three** cons of cloud storage.
6. Explain the difference between a NAS and cloud storage.
7. Describe how to update a graphics driver.
## Practical tasks
1. Change the mouse pointer to a large black scheme and add the “This PC” icon to the desktop; then restore the original settings.
2. Open Device Manager and list the display adapter, audio device and network adapter on your computer.
